source.title: Does Double Descent Occur in Self-Supervised Learning?
source.authors: A. Lupidi; Yonatan Gideoni; D. Jayalath

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests for double descent in self-supervised autoencoders and reports that the expected test-loss peak is absent in its experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own autoencoder test-loss and training-loss results. Results attributed to cited studies are not included. Test-loss values are presented in figures and described qualitatively in the text; the paper does not give their numerical values.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own model-width and dataset-size sweeps on self-supervised autoencoders and reports test loss. It argues the double-descent peak does not occur there, which bears directly on V1, V3 and V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also conjecture the discrepancy may stem from formulation: supervised learning assumes noisy data, while self-supervised learning learns a distribution. They call for theory and more extensive experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses self-supervised autoencoders on artificial data, varying latent width, hidden width, or dataset size; its reconstruction objective is MSE. It is not a reproduction of the original supervised deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The standard AE result depends on which dimension is varied: latent-width scaling gives a U-shaped loss, while hidden-width scaling gives a decreasing loss.
record.peer_reviewed: HLD 2023: 1st Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics
record.problems: The experiments use artificial data and only standard and linear autoencoders. Test-loss curves are largely reported qualitatively through figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates; the authors themselves call for more extensive experiments.

untested.parts: Supervised deep networks, label noise, real data, deeper or convolutional architectures.
Not tested: no epoch-wise test-loss curve.
Only a linear autoencoder on low-noise synthetic data; no nonlinear or supervised sample-wise sweep.
Only autoencoders; no other model classes such as random features or trees.
Not tested: SNR fixed at 10, and no noise or regularization sweep.

record.verdict_notes: I chose limits_scope rather than challenges because the absence is shown only in a narrow setting the authors frame as outside the supervised regime: synthetic, low-noise (SNR 10), self-supervised autoencoders. The evidence is qualitative, from figures only, with no uncertainty estimates. The low noise level may matter given V6: noise drives the peak, and the paper does not vary noise. The authors note that Dubova did observe double descent in an autoencoder. They also acknowledge ambiguity about the output size that defines the interpolation threshold.

versions.untested_parts: Tests model-size sweeps in self-supervised autoencoders only; it does not test supervised deep networks generally.
No test-loss sweep over training epochs is reported.
Tests a linear autoencoder while varying dataset size; the paper does not report a separate analysis focused specifically on a narrowly identified interpolation threshold.
Tests standard and linear autoencoders in self-supervised settings, not a broad range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as a predictor of peak locations across axes.
No systematic test of label-noise or regularization effects, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization is reported.
The study does not re-express the curve using an effective parameter count.

relationships.condition: Self-supervised nonlinear autoencoder, synthetic Gaussian data, SNR 10, width sweeps
relationships.reason: The test loss is U-shaped over latent width (R1) and decreases monotonically over hidden width (R2), even though interpolation is reached (R3, R4). This marks a setting where model-wise double descent is not seen.
relationships.display_finding: Despite reaching interpolation, test loss was U-shaped over latent width and decreased monotonically over hidden width.

relationships.condition: Linear autoencoder, dataset size from 8 to 1.1e6, synthetic data
relationships.reason: No discernible interpolation peak appears as sample size varies (R5), so sample-wise harm is not seen in this self-supervised setting.
relationships.display_finding: Varying dataset size produces no discernible interpolation peak or harmful sample-size region.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Linear autoencoder, dataset size from 8 to 1.1e6, synthetic data
source_check.reason: R5 identifies a tested setting without a discernible sample-wise interpolation peak. This qualifies the applicability of V3's possibility claim; it does not refute that more data can hurt elsewhere or establish absence of every possible local increase.

relationships.reason: No second descent past interpolation appears; the classical U-shape or monotone decrease is seen instead (R1, R2, R5). This restricts the claimed generality across model classes.
relationships.display_finding: No second descent appeared beyond interpolation; error instead followed a classical U-shape or decreased monotonically.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R1 explicitly lacks the predicted second descent despite reaching interpolation, challenging the general capacity-wise curve in the standard autoencoder. R2 also lacks the double-descent shape. The linear-autoencoder result R5 varies samples rather than capacity and should be excluded from this V4 condition group.

relation.reason: The authors measure test loss while varying autoencoder widths and, separately, training-set size to search for double descent.

tranche.reason: The study presents its own negative experiments and argues that double descent may fail in self-supervised settings.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased and explicitly calls for further theory and experiments. The nonlinear AE uses SNR 10, data latent dimension 20, 50 features and 200 epochs; Figure 1 uses irregular sampling with nearest-point coloring.

statements.correction: Fixed linear autoencoder; synthetic data; no discernible interpolation peak in the sample-size sweep; linear-experiment SNR not stated in Table 2.
statements.problem: The absent sample-wise peak is supported, but the linear-autoencoder experiment is not explicitly identified as low-noise.
